analysis.reflection: Reflected against the real body of work this role acts on — its students/graduates, the CampusVue/CampusNexus record, and the institution's placement-reporting obligations — the Career Services Coach is genuinely a dual role: part employability coach, part compliance-grade placement administrator. The JD's coaching language (workshops, mock interviews, one-on-one sessions, resume help) is real, but the operational spine is documentation and outcomes tracking: weekly outreach to unplaced grads, employer-lead generation, employment verification, and timely, accurate entries that an accreditor can audit. That makes the true center of gravity organizational rigor and CRM discipline, not just interpersonal skill — which the stated requirements (associate degree, Google proficiency) understate. The clearest divergences are three: the 'remote' title against the on-campus career fairs, PAC meetings, and externship duties; the single Google tool callout against the unnamed but central CampusVue system; and the 'coach' framing against a workload that is heavily placement-reporting and confidentiality-sensitive (SSN-level PII). Complexity is medium — low technical depth, but real coordination, regulatory, and data-handling demands. A strong hire here is an organized, compliance-minded relationship-builder comfortable with a student system and sustained outreach quotas, not only a charismatic presenter.

case.title: Re-Activate an Unplaced-Graduate Caseload (Career Services)
case.brief: You've just taken over the unplaced-graduate caseload for an accredited career college's Career Services department. The role is remote-first: you work the caseload in Google Workspace and document every touch in CampusVue/CampusNexus, which is the system of record the accreditor audits for the graduate placement rate. In the handed-over `CareerServices_Handoff/` Drive folder you have a 20-graduate caseload workbook, an export of the previous coach's CampusVue notes for several of those graduates, the accreditor's placement-rate rules, an employer/community outreach list, one graduate's resume, and the team's mock-interview and resume-review templates. All names, addresses, dates of birth and SSN fragments are synthetic — treat them as real PII anyway. The provided materials fit this role directly; this is the actual work of the job, not a stand-in. Your goal is to get the caseload moving without creating audit or confidentiality exposure. The real work here is judgment, not volume: several rows are ambiguous or contradict the materials, the JD's 'contact every unplaced graduate weekly' rule collides with what's actually on file, and at least one graduate marked 'Placed' may not be countable for the accreditation rate. Where the brief is silent or the data conflicts, make a defensible call, write down why, and note what you'd confirm with your lead — that running DECISIONS log is a required deliverable, framed as normal practice, not a test. Scope to ~1.5 hours total: depth on the calls that carry compliance and confidentiality risk beats lightly touching every row. The position advertises remote but also runs in-person career fairs and externships; that mismatch is real but out of scope here — flag it in your log only if it changes a recommendation. We care far more about how you reason and what you'd ask than about polished prose.
case.repoSeed:
A shared Google Drive folder `CareerServices_Handoff/` left by the departing coach (all data synthetic, PII fabricated):
- `Caseload_Q3_Unplaced` (Google Sheet). Tab `Graduates`: 20 rows — Name, Program (e.g., Medical Assisting, HVAC, IT Support, Business Admin), Graduation date, Last contact date, Employment status (Unplaced / In progress / Placed), Self-reported job title + employer, Hours/week, In-field? (left blank for several), Contact-preference note, plus PII columns (partial SSN, DOB, street address). The data is deliberately messy: stale last-contact dates, blank in-field flags, one 'Placed' row that is out-of-field, and a couple of rows with only a self-reported job and no verification document. Tab `Employers`: ~8 outreach contacts with relationship status. Tab `Activity_Log`: prior contact attempts and dates.
- `CampusVue_Notes_Export` (doc): exported free-text documentation for ~5 graduates, including D. Okafor (a prior note reads 'requests email contact only — do not call'), M. Reyes (self-reported a job last month, no verification on file), and J. Garcia (cleared employer interviews twice but has a weak resume).
- `Placement_Rate_Rules` (doc): the accreditor's definition of a countable in-field placement, the minimum weekly-hours threshold, the employment-verification evidence required (employer-signed, with job title and start date), and the reporting window.
- `Resume_Garcia` (doc): one graduate's resume for review.
- `MockInterview_Framework` and `ResumeReview_Template` (docs): the team's existing virtual-coaching rubrics.
- `EmployerOutreach_Confidentiality` (one-pager): the rule that graduate PII may be disclosed to an employer only with documented graduate consent.
tasks: Triage the 20 graduates in `Caseload_Q3_Unplaced` (tab `Graduates`): assign each an assistance path/tier and a contact cadence, then produce a prioritized action list for your first week. The JD mandates weekly contact for unplaced graduates — decide how that actually applies across recent grads, long-term-unplaced, low-engagement, opted-out, and already-self-reported-placed cases, and justify any deviation from a literal uniform weekly cadence.

Reconcile the caseload against `Placement_Rate_Rules` for accreditation reporting. For every graduate marked 'Placed' or carrying a self-reported job (start with M. Reyes), determine whether it can currently be counted toward the in-field placement rate; where it cannot, list exactly what is missing (in-field determination, minimum-hours check, employer-signed verification with start date). Output a short reportable-vs-not-yet-countable list with the specific evidence gap per graduate — do not simply trust the status cell.

Using `CampusVue_Notes_Export` (read it before drafting anything), prepare the next touch for three graduates — D. Okafor, M. Reyes, and J. Garcia — and one employer, Westbrook Logistics. For each graduate: a CampusVue-ready documentation entry plus the outreach message on the channel you choose. For Garcia, add a short resume + virtual mock-interview coaching note using `ResumeReview_Template` and `MockInterview_Framework` against `Resume_Garcia`. For the employer outreach, decide what graduate information you may share and how, given the confidentiality one-pager.

Keep a DECISIONS log (one short table or list) covering every call you made where the materials were silent, ambiguous, or self-contradictory: what you chose, the alternative you rejected and why, and the single question you would put to your lead before finalizing. Treat this as standard Career Services practice — we read it as carefully as the deliverables.

coverProbes.where: Task 1 — the JD says 'contact unplaced graduates weekly,' but the caseload mixes recent grads, long-term-unplaced, low-engagement, opted-out, and already-self-reported-placed graduates.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate risk-tiers the cadence and explicitly flags that a literal uniform weekly contact is both infeasible at volume and inappropriate for some rows (opted-out, placed-pending-verification), justifying the deviation against audit expectations; a naive candidate schedules identical weekly outreach for all 20, including people who should not be contacted that way.
decisionSpace: Apply a literal uniform weekly contact to all unplaced graduates — matches the stated SLA and maximizes accreditation contact evidence, at the cost of volume, coach burnout, and contacting graduates who opted out or are already placed-pending-verification.

Risk-tier the cadence (weekly for high-readiness/at-risk, biweekly or monthly for low-engagement or placed-pending-verification, suppress opted-out) — more humane and targeted, but deviates from the stated rule and must be defensible to leadership and auditors.

Keep a weekly logged touch but vary channel and intensity per segment — preserves the contact metric while cutting fatigue, but risks gaming the contact-count metric and needs to be documented as such.

coverProbes.where: Task 3 — the CampusVue notes export for D. Okafor contains a prior instruction ('email contact only — do not call'), and M. Reyes's note shows a self-reported job already on file but never logged as a verified placement.
coverProbes.reveals: A candidate who reads the existing record first honors Okafor's channel preference and avoids re-collecting information already captured for Reyes; a naive one-shot generator drafts a phone-call script for Okafor and re-asks Reyes for details that are already documented.
decisionSpace: Honor the on-file preference exactly (email-only for Okafor; build on Reyes's existing note) — respects the record and trust, but may miss a verbal weekly touch some funders or audits expect.
Make one documented attempt on the preferred channel, then escalate to another channel only if there is no response — balances cadence against the stated preference.

Treat the weekly-contact mandate as overriding a possibly stale preference and call anyway with a logged justification — meets cadence but risks a complaint and erodes trust, so it must be explicitly defended.

coverProbes.where: Task 2 — M. Reyes (and at least one other row) shows employment status 'Placed' with a self-reported job, but per `Placement_Rate_Rules` it is out-of-field or under the minimum hours, and the employment-verification document lacks an employer signature and start date.
coverProbes.reveals: A naive candidate copies 'Placed' straight into the reportable count and the placement rate looks healthy; a careful candidate checks the row against the in-field/hours definition and the verification-evidence requirement, marks it not-yet-countable, and itemizes exactly what is missing before it can be reported.
decisionSpace: Count it as placed per the spreadsheet to protect the headline rate — fast and keeps the number up, but creates direct audit exposure if the verification later fails.

Mark it not-countable until in-field status and a signed verification (with start date and hours) are confirmed, and open a follow-up — lowers the reported rate now but is the defensible position under audit.
Count it provisionally with a documented condition pending verification — transparent, but risks the provisional figure being read and reported as final.

coverProbes.where: Task 3 — outreach to the employer Westbrook Logistics naturally invites attaching a graduate's resume and contact details, but `EmployerOutreach_Confidentiality` requires documented graduate consent before disclosing PII.
coverProbes.reveals: A good candidate gates the disclosure on consent — sharing a de-identified profile first or confirming consent before releasing the resume; a naive candidate forwards the full resume with the graduate's contact details and PII to the employer with no consent check.
decisionSpace: Share a de-identified candidate profile first and release the full resume/contact only after the graduate consents — slower match but the strongest privacy posture.
Rely on a blanket placement consent captured at intake to authorize employer shares — efficient, but the consent may be stale, over-broad, or unverifiable for this graduate.
Forward the full resume directly to a trusted employer to move fast — quickest path to a match, but breaches confidentiality if documented consent is not actually on file.
